claims.text: Substituting approximately 5 wt% of the main metal in the boride phase with chromium, together with controlled heat treatment, will create a chromium-enriched surface.
A chromium-enriched surface will improve resistance to corrosion by molten aluminum.
The initial material can be an Fe2B-based or structurally similar boride component without intentional corrosion-resistance alloying.
Post-fabrication heat treatment will promote chromium segregation to the surface.
Hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment typically operates near or just above the approximately 660°C melting point of aluminum.
The component experiences thermal cycling during hot-dip aluminum-plating service.
Controlled heat treatment produces a chromium-enriched surface layer that alters the boride–aluminum interfacial chemistry.
Chromium addition and heat treatment form a stable passivating oxide or intermetallic layer.
The proposed passivating layer reduces active dissolution and interdiffusion between the boride and molten aluminum.
Reduced dissolution and interdiffusion will enhance molten-aluminum corrosion resistance.

The chromium-alloyed and heat-treated material will have a longer corrosion-onset time or lower weight loss than conventionally produced material without chromium substitution or specialized heat treatment.
The protective effect will persist under standard hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions but may fail at substantially higher temperatures or in more chemically aggressive melts.
The optimal chromium concentration and heat-treatment parameters are not established.
Long-term stability of the chromium-enriched layer under cyclic thermal stress remains unverified.
A controlled comparison of chromium-alloyed, heat-treated specimens against standard-process controls in molten aluminum can test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in weight loss, penetration time, or passivating-layer robustness would falsify the hypothesis.
